D1 research authoring, batch 87 (2026-09-27): two ASSOCIATION_ONLY draft mappings added at ranks 1-2 (depressive-disorder, anxiety-disorder) pending qualified-human citation verification under docs/citation-verification-sop.md; mapping approval is not citation verification. The two edges SHARE ONE EVIDENCE SET of three studies because the located non-melanoma psychosocial literature is three studies in total and all three measure anxiety and depression together in the same participants. They are NOT independent lines of evidence and are registered as one evidence set supporting two targets, which is why the anxiety edge is ranked second.

SCOPE RESOLUTION, APPLIED TO BOTH EDGES: this catalog identity is named the bare 'Squamous cell carcinoma' with no site qualifier and no alias, which on its face is an UMBRELLA. It is resolved to CUTANEOUS AND MUCO-CUTANEOUS squamous cell carcinoma on three pieces of recorded evidence, namely its catalog body system of Skin Conditions, its rating schedule citation of 38 CFR 4.118, which is the skin rating framework, and the seven already-registered explicit incoming edges from lichen-sclerosus, actinic-keratosis, bowen-s-disease, erythroplasia-of-queyrat, lichen-planus, median-rhomboid-glossitis and necrobiosis-lipoidica, every one of which is a dermatologic or mucocutaneous precursor. The commonest squamous cell carcinomas overall, in lung, cervix and oesophagus, are therefore NOT within this identity, and the catalog already carries respiratory-cancer, laryngeal-cancer, oral-cancer and esophageal-cancer as separate identities. Any individual claim MUST state the cutaneous or mucocutaneous site.

HISTOLOGY-MIX DISCLOSURE, APPLIED TO BOTH EDGES: all three anchors on both edges enrol MIXED BASAL AND SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA patients and none separates the two histologies, so the psychological findings cannot be attributed to this identity specifically. This is stated on the face of each edge and not only in the reference notes.

RECURRENCE-FEAR MEASUREMENT GAP: the single most prevalent concern identified by the anchors is fear of tumour recurrence, which is measured by recurrence-specific instruments rather than by the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, so the anxiety captured on these edges MAY UNDERSTATE recurrence-related anxiety specifically. No located anchor in this batch uses a recurrence-specific instrument.

TWO WITHHELD ROUTES, both recorded rather than forced. (1) burn-scar carcinoma as DIRECTION REVERSAL: the systematic review of skin cancer arising from burn scars reports a mean latency of 21.7 years from burn to cancer, with squamous cell carcinoma the commonest malignancy at 67.19 percent, so the causal arrow runs from the burn to this identity and an edge in this identity's own name direction would have asserted the reverse. (2) perineural invasion as MECHANISM-VOCABULARY MISMATCH: perineural invasion is TUMOUR SPREAD ALONG a nerve, not a neuropathy of that nerve, and the located evidence is strong on it, 19.1 percent recurrence against 5.6 percent without and p EQUALS 0.005, but no catalog identity represents it, and registering peripheral-neuropathy would have converted a prognostic feature into a nerve disease.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: Psychological distress is the one documented accompaniment of this identity that the catalog can carry, and the located non-melanoma psychosocial literature reports it three times over. In a cross-sectional study of 56 patients with basal cell carcinoma and/or squamous cell carcinoma at a skin cancer clinic, the most prevalent concerns were WORRIES ABOUT TUMOUR RECURRENCE and THE POTENTIAL SIZE AND CONSPICUOUSNESS OF THE SCAR, and SKIN CANCER-SPECIFIC QUALITY-OF-LIFE CONCERNS SIGNIFICANTLY PREDICTED DISTRESS MANIFESTING THROUGH ANXIOUS AND DEPRESSIVE SYMPTOMOLOGY, with the social concerns related to the disease being the most significant predictor of distress (PMID 24368239). A cross-sectional study of 60 consecutive patients with squamous and/or basal cell carcinoma, assessed with the Skin Cancer Index, the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale and the Supportive Care Needs survey, found that MORE THAN HALF indicated unmet needs, most frequently for help with PREVENTION OF FUTURE SKIN CANCERS and with the health system and informational matters, that PSYCHOLOGICAL NEEDS WERE STRONGLY ASSOCIATED with skin cancer-specific and general distress, and that HIGHER LEVELS OF ANXIOUS AND DEPRESSIVE SYMPTOMS WERE RELATED TO GREATER PATIENT NEEDS ACROSS ALL DOMAINS, despite the authors' framing that non-melanoma skin cancer is NOT LIFE THREATENING IN MOST CASES (PMID 26236032). A study of 54 heterosexual couples in which one partner had been diagnosed with a skin cancer within the previous 12 months found SIMILAR DISTRESS LEVELS IN PATIENTS AND SPOUSES, that PATIENTS' DEPRESSION PREDICTED SPOUSES' DEPRESSION and that SPOUSES' ANXIETY PREDICTED PATIENTS' ANXIETY, and that spouses of patients with melanoma reported significantly higher distress than spouses of patients with non-melanoma skin cancer (PMID 38959518). Recorded as documented association only, with the fact that all three anchors enrol mixed basal and squamous cell populations, carried openly.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual, and ALL THREE ANCHORS ENROL MIXED BASAL AND SQUAMOUS CELL POPULATIONS rather than this identity alone, which is the central limitation of this edge and is stated first: no located source in this batch reports a psychological outcome in a squamous cell carcinoma population that is separated from basal cell carcinoma, so the distress levels cannot be attributed to this identity specifically and the edge is registered as a non-melanoma skin cancer finding applied to a cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma identity with that mapping disclosed. All three anchors are CROSS-SECTIONAL and SELF-SELECTED, and the largest is a single skin cancer clinic sample of 56 and 60 patients respectively. The third anchor is a COUPLE STUDY, so its central finding is a dyadic one, that distress is mutual between partners, and that dyadic finding cannot be reduced to a property of the patient alone; its melanoma comparison also places this identity's cohort in the lower-distress group, which is a relative and not an absolute figure. DIRECTION IS ALSO PARTLY CONTRADICTED WITHIN THE LOCATED EVIDENCE, because the first anchor reports that the concerns which PREDICT distress are worry about recurrence and the scar, that is anticipatory responses to the disease, while the third reports that a partner's mood PREDICTS the patient's mood, so the located set contains both disease-to-mood and mood-to-mood pathways and cannot settle the direction for an individual. Individual claims require a dated histopathologically confirmed cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma with the site and the differentiation grade recorded, a structured depression instrument administered and scored with the instrument and its threshold named, an explicit timeline distinguishing mood symptoms that predate the diagnosis from those that follow it, an assessment of the functional and cosmetic impact of the resection site, and a clinical determination separating a depressive disorder from anticipatory distress about recurrence, from adjustment to a visible scar, from a pre-existing mood disorder and from distress attributable to a concurrent or prior cancer diagnosis.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: The hypothesised vector is anticipatory threat maintained by an unresolved recurrence risk: in this disease local recurrence is a live possibility that the patient cannot self-assess, so the patient must remain in a state of surveillance without a point at which the risk can be considered closed, and the surveillance state is what generates the recurring worry the first anchor identifies as the most prevalent concern; that worry sustains a background of low mood, the visible or conspicuous resection scar adds a social-evaluative load, and the combined anticipatory and social load is what the first anchor reports as predicting depressive symptomology, so the vector is named as the unresolved-surveillance-and-social-evaluative loop rather than as a shared biological substrate.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: Authored at ASSOCIATION_ONLY at single-clinic-cross-sectional-cohort, consecutive-sample-cross-sectional-cohort and dyadic-couple-cross-sectional-study class, following the file's existing dermatological, oncological and psychological pathway scope. The 56-patient cohort is the anchor that supplies the content of the distress, namely that the most prevalent concerns are recurrence worry and scar conspicuousness and that skin-cancer-specific concerns significantly predict anxious and depressive symptomology, which is what makes the mechanism claim concrete rather than generic (PMID 24368239). The 60-patient cohort is registered for its needs analysis, that more than half reported unmet needs and that higher anxious and depressive symptoms were related to greater needs across all domains, and for the authors' own explicit framing that this is not a life-threatening disease in most cases, which is the located reason the distress is not dismissed (PMID 26236032). The couple study is registered for the dyadic finding, that patients' depression predicted spouses' depression and vice versa, which is the located evidence that the burden is relational and not confined to the patient, and its melanoma-versus-non-melanoma comparison is disclosed (PMID 38959518). Because all three anchors enrol mixed basal and squamous populations and none is a cohort study, the conservative standard holds the edge at association only and states no distress rate for this identity.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: ALL THREE ANCHORS ENROL MIXED BASAL AND SQUAMOUS CELL POPULATIONS: no located source reports a psychological outcome in a squamous cell carcinoma population SEPARATED FROM BASAL CELL CARCINOMA, so the distress levels cannot be attributed to this identity specifically and the edge is a NON-MELANOMA SKIN CANCER finding applied to a cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma identity with that mapping disclosed (PMID 24368239, PMID 26236032, PMID 38959518). ALL THREE ANCHORS ARE CROSS-SECTIONAL AND CLINIC-BASED, with samples of 56 and 60 patients from single skin cancer clinics, so neither is a population sample and neither supports a prevalence (PMID 24368239, PMID 26236032). DIRECTION IS CONTRADICTED WITHIN THE LOCATED SET: the first anchor reports that the concerns PREDICTING distress are recurrence worry and scar conspicuousness, that is anticipatory responses to the disease, while the third reports that a SPOUSE'S MOOD PREDICTED THE PATIENT'S MOOD, so the located evidence contains both a disease-to-mood and a mood-to-mood pathway and cannot settle the direction for an individual (PMID 24368239, PMID 38959518). THE THIRD ANCHOR IS A DYADIC STUDY, so its central finding is that distress is MUTUAL BETWEEN PARTNERS, and that finding cannot be reduced to a property of the patient alone; its melanoma comparison also places this cohort in the LOWER-distress group of the two, which is a RELATIVE rather than an absolute figure and provides no non-cancer reference (PMID 38959518). THE TWO ANCHORS IN DIFFERENT COUNTRIES AND CLINICAL SETTINGS REPORT CONVERGENT QUALITATIVE CONCERNS but no shared instrument, scale or threshold, so the numerical similarity between them cannot be assumed. NO located anchor reports a depression DIAGNOSIS rate, reports a longitudinal course, or assesses whether excision, follow-up or any treatment changes distress; none distinguishes distress attributable to this diagnosis from distress attributable to a prior or concurrent cancer, which the second anchor's phrase ASSOCIATED WITH AN INCREASED RISK FOR OTHER CANCERS makes a live alternative in this population.
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Distress attributable to a prior or concurrent cancer diagnosis, which the located non-melanoma literature's own framing of an increased risk of further cancers makes a live alternative explanation in a heavily pre-screened population
Adjustment disorder to a visible or disfiguring resection scar, which the first anchor identifies as one of the two most prevalent concerns and which is a different diagnosis with a different course
A pre-existing mood disorder predating the diagnosis, which the cross-sectional design of all three anchors cannot temporally separate

Fear of cancer recurrence as a distinct construct from depression, which the first anchor identifies as the most prevalent concern and which is measured by different instruments and is not interchangeable with a depressive disorder
Distress arising from a spouse's or family's own cancer history, which the dyadic anchor identifies as a bidirectional contributor and which no located anchor controls for

sourceReferences.citation: Radiotis G, Roberts N, Czajkowska Z, et al. Nonmelanoma skin cancer: disease-specific quality-of-life concerns and distress. Oncol Nurs Forum. 2014 Jan 1;41(1):57-65. doi: 10.1188/14.ONF.57-65. PMID 24368239.
sourceReferences.note: CROSS-SECTIONAL STUDY OF 56 PATIENTS WITH BASAL CELL CARCINOMA AND/OR SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA at a skin cancer clinic, measuring the importance of appearance, psychological distress and quality of life with quantitative self-report data. THE MOST PREVALENT CONCERNS WERE WORRIES ABOUT TUMOUR RECURRENCE AND THE POTENTIAL SIZE AND CONSPICUOUSNESS OF THE SCAR. SKIN CANCER-SPECIFIC QUALITY-OF-LIFE CONCERNS SIGNIFICANTLY PREDICTED DISTRESS MANIFESTING THROUGH ANXIOUS AND DEPRESSIVE SYMPTOMOLOGY, and the social concerns related to the disease were the MOST SIGNIFICANT PREDICTOR of distress. The authors conclude that the findings give healthcare professionals a broad picture of the most prevalent non-melanoma skin cancer-specific concerns and emphasise the often-overlooked psychosocial effects of the disease. Registered as the anchor that supplies the CONTENT of the distress, which is what makes the mechanism claim concrete. DISCLOSED: the sample is MIXED BASAL AND SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA and is not separated by histology, and it is a single-clinic cross-sectional sample of 56.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: Oncol Nurs Forum. 2014;41(1):57-65. Cross-sectional study of 56 patients with basal and/or squamous cell carcinoma: the most prevalent concerns were recurrence worry and scar size and conspicuousness, and skin cancer-specific quality-of-life concerns significantly predicted anxious and depressive symptomology.

sourceReferences.citation: Körner A, Garland R, Czajkowska Z, et al. Supportive care needs and distress in patients with non-melanoma skin cancer: Nothing to worry about?. Eur J Oncol Nurs. 2016 Feb;20:150-5. doi: 10.1016/j.ejon.2015.07.006. PMID 26236032.
sourceReferences.note: CROSS-SECTIONAL STUDY OF 60 CONSECUTIVE PATIENTS WITH SQUAMOUS AND/OR BASAL CELL CARCINOMA, assessed with the Skin Cancer Index, the HOSPITAL ANXIETY AND DEPRESSION SCALE, the Supportive Care Needs survey, an inquiry on informational needs regarding skin cancer prevention and a socio-demographic questionnaire. MORE THAN HALF OF THE PATIENTS INDICATED UNMET NEEDS, most frequently endorsing moderate and high needs for help with THE PREVENTION OF FUTURE SKIN CANCERS and with the health system and informational matters. PSYCHOLOGICAL NEEDS WERE STRONGLY ASSOCIATED with skin cancer-specific and general distress, and HIGHER LEVELS OF ANXIOUS AND DEPRESSIVE SYMPTOMS WERE RELATED TO GREATER PATIENT NEEDS ACROSS ALL DOMAINS. The authors open by noting the paucity of psychosocial research on non-melanoma skin cancer, state that these malignancies mainly develop on the head and neck, frequently recur and are associated with an increased risk for other cancers, and conclude that despite non-melanoma skin cancer NOT BEING LIFE THREATENING IN MOST CASES there is a significant proportion of patients with unmet supportive care needs and heightened distress. Registered for the needs analysis and for the authors' explicit framing that the disease is not usually life-threatening, which is the located reason the distress is not dismissed. DISCLOSED: MIXED squamous and basal population, single-centre, cross-sectional, no control group.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: Eur J Oncol Nurs. 2016;20(2):150-155. Cross-sectional study of 60 consecutive patients with squamous and/or basal cell carcinoma using the Skin Cancer Index, HADS and Supportive Care Needs survey: more than half reported unmet needs, psychological needs were strongly associated with skin cancer-specific and general distress, and higher anxious and depressive symptoms related to greater needs across all domains.

sourceReferences.citation: Sauer C, Ullerich C, Livingstone E, et al. Psychosocial distress and psychosocial resources in couples facing non-melanoma skin cancers and malignant melanoma. J Psychosoc Oncol. 2025;43(2):173-188. doi: 10.1080/07347332.2024.2371344. PMID 38959518.
sourceReferences.note: QUANTITATIVE CROSS-SECTIONAL STUDY OF 54 HETEROSEXUAL COUPLES in which one partner had been diagnosed with a non-melanoma skin cancer or malignant melanoma WITHIN THE PREVIOUS 12 MONTHS, with patients and spouses reporting depression and anxiety on the HOSPITAL ANXIETY AND DEPRESSION SCALE, psychosocial resources within the last four weeks and last three years on the Essen Resource Inventory, and partnership quality on a short Partnership Questionnaire, analysed by multiple regression for dyadic dynamics. SIMILAR DISTRESS LEVELS WERE FOUND IN PATIENTS AND SPOUSES, as well as in patients with different skin cancers. SPOUSES FROM PATIENTS WITH MELANOMA REPORTED SIGNIFICANTLY HIGHER DISTRESS than spouses of patients with non-melanoma skin cancer. PATIENTS' DEPRESSION PREDICTED SPOUSES' DEPRESSION and SPOUSES' ANXIETY PREDICTED PATIENTS' ANXIETY, and personal resources were indicated as a DISTRESS BUFFER. The authors conclude that the psychological interdependencies between patients' and spouses' depression and anxiety highlight the importance of a DYADIC PERSPECTIVE and of couple interventions. Registered for the dyadic finding, which is the located evidence that the burden is relational. DISCLOSED: a COUPLE STUDY whose central result is mutual rather than patient-level, and whose melanoma comparison gives a RELATIVE rather than an absolute figure with no non-cancer reference.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: J Psychosoc Oncol. 2025;43(2):173-188. Cross-sectional dyadic study of 54 couples facing non-melanoma skin cancer or melanoma: similar distress in patients and spouses, patients' depression predicting spouses' depression and spouses' anxiety predicting patients' anxiety, and personal resources acting as a distress buffer.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: This edge shares its entire anchor set with the depressive-disorder edge, and that sharing is the located finding rather than a convenience: the non-melanoma skin cancer psychosocial literature located in this batch is three studies in total, and all three measure BOTH anxious and depressive symptoms with the same instrument, so the two edges are NOT INDEPENDENT lines of evidence and are registered as one evidence set supporting two targets. The content is the same. The 56-patient clinic sample found that skin cancer-specific quality-of-life concerns significantly predicted distress manifesting through anxious and depressive symptomology, and identified the most prevalent concerns as worries about tumour recurrence and the potential size and conspicuousness of the scar (PMID 24368239). The 60-patient consecutive sample found that psychological needs were strongly associated with skin cancer-specific and general distress, and that higher levels of anxious and depressive symptoms were related to greater patient needs across all domains (PMID 26236032). The 54-couple study found similar distress levels in patients and spouses, that spouses' anxiety predicted patients' anxiety, and that spouses of patients with melanoma reported significantly higher distress than spouses of patients with non-melanoma skin cancer (PMID 38959518). Recorded as documented association only, with the fact that the anxiety-specific evidence is thinner than the mood evidence generally, carried openly.
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established for any individual, and THE SHARED ANCHOR SET IS THE FIRST LIMITATION: all three anchors measure anxiety and depression TOGETHER on the same instrument in the same participants, so this edge contains NO ANCHOR THAT REPORTS AN ANXIETY OUTCOME ALONE, and the anxiety content is a secondary stratum of a distress measure rather than a finding about anxiety in its own right. All three anchors enrol MIXED BASAL AND SQUAMOUS CELL POPULATIONS and none separates the two histologies, so the finding cannot be attributed to this identity. All three are CROSS-SECTIONAL and CLINIC-BASED, with samples of 56 and 60 patients, and the third is a DYADIC study in which the anxiety result of interest is that a SPOUSE'S ANXIETY PREDICTED THE PATIENT'S ANXIETY, which is a relation between two people rather than a property of the disease, and which cannot support a claim that this identity produces anxiety in the patient. A FURTHER LIMITATION IS SPECIFIC TO ANXIETY AND IS RECORDED RATHER THAN SMOOTHED: fear of cancer recurrence, which the first anchor identifies as the single most prevalent concern, is measured by recurrence-specific instruments rather than by the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, so the anxiety reported by these three anchors may understate recurrence-related anxiety specifically, and no located anchor in this batch uses a recurrence-specific instrument. Individual claims require a dated histopathologically confirmed cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma with site and grade recorded, a structured anxiety instrument administered and scored with the instrument and its threshold named, a SEPARATE recurrence-specific measure where recurrence fear is at issue, an explicit timeline distinguishing anxiety that predates the diagnosis from that which follows it, and a clinical determination separating an anxiety disorder from anticipatory fear of recurrence, from social anxiety about a visible scar, from a pre-existing anxiety disorder and from anxiety attributable to a concurrent or prior cancer diagnosis.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: The hypothesised vector is anticipatory hypervigilance sustained by an unverifiable risk: the patient cannot observe whether a recurrence has occurred, so vigilance must persist between appointments, and a vigilance state that cannot be discharged produces persistent physiological arousal which presents as anxiety symptoms; the visible or conspicuous resection scar adds a social-evaluative threat channel to the same vigilance, and the located evidence that social concerns were the most significant predictor of distress is what makes the social channel rather than the somatic one the primary named vector. The vector is named as this evaluative-and-anticipatory channel rather than as a shared biological substrate, because no located anchor measures any biological variable and because the located evidence is a psychosocial measurement exercise.
